name: Ben Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58 and lead the carpenters making temporary stairs and handrails on a civic building site. My vocational trade certificate led to years of work, and I'm among the best at spotting a rail that will move, though the pay is the normal trade rate. I like a safe handover; chasing a rushed schedule wears me out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and do you use AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works at a postal office and our children are grown. We have about four months of expenses saved and some other contractors nearby. I have never used AI and prefer my site notebook; I attend union safety meetings, and I hope to leave regular site work around 67 if retirement income covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the stair crew the office can finish its paperwork faster, while we keep the temporary handrail solid. Our work will still be judged by whether someone can use the stairs safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lead the site carpenters and earn the normal trade wage. My partner's postal-office income is steady, our children are grown and we have about four months of expenses saved; retirement around 67 is a hope, not a paid-for fact yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep building temporary stairs and checking their handrails at the civic building site. At the next workplace union meeting I'll ask for paid time to teach apprentices a proper rail-load check rather than letting quicker checklists replace practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the job in this mild picture. I still need to put our retirement numbers alongside the bills before choosing a final work date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did a checklist miss a rail fault?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week a handrail was marked complete on the sheet but rocked against its fixing. We tightened the temporary stair anchor before other trades used the handrail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the paid apprentice hour involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The lesson would give two apprentices a paid hour on a grounded test stair with an experienced fitter. I'll ask the union group to put those hours into the builder's rota.

say: **Temporary stairs** still need a physical handrail check on every busy building floor.
Faster **office checklists** should not replace paid apprentice practice.
think: My **normal trade wage** and partner's postal work keep current bills covered.
Four months of **saved expenses** help, but retirement figures still need checking.
do: **Build** civic-site temporary stairs and test every handrail fixing.
**Request** paid apprentice rail checks at workplace union meeting.
feel: **Calm** about current work, cautious about later retirement income.
S0.quote: We tightened the temporary stair anchor before other trades used the handrail.
fieldNote: He caught a **loose handrail** on a real stair after paperwork marked it complete.
The **union training request** specifies paid apprentice time and a grounded practice stair; current household wages support calm.

steps.text: Build civic-site temporary stairs and test handrail fixings
Request paid apprentice rail checks at workplace union meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI can write plans and order brackets before a robot climbs a temporary stair. The builder must let a fitter reject a plan that leaves a rail loose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own lead role still looks secure while office tasks change, though I worry about young workers being sent into shorter rushed shifts. We have four months saved and some nearby builders, so I can push back without losing sleep over next week's pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep a written log of rail fixes on the next two civic-site floors. At the union safety meeting I'll ask for a named worker to sign off each temporary stair before an AI schedule moves another trade onto it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about a rushed site handover, with my own wage safe for now. I don't use AI tools and would rather make the safety rule clear than learn a new screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do at a loose rail?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put a load on the rail and call the foreman if the anchor shifted. A computer's green mark cannot hold a temporary stair rail under a worker's hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the written log support a site rule?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The log would show the floor, anchor, fault and paid time spent fixing it. The union representative can use those records to ask the builder for a real inspection slot.

say: **AI plans** can speed office work before robots build stairs.
A trained fitter needs **sign-off authority** over temporary handrails.
think: My **lead wage** looks secure for now.
Shorter **apprentice shifts** and rushed handovers could make the site less safe.
do: **Record** rail faults and fixing time on two civic-site floors.
**Ask** union safety meeting for named worker stair sign-off.
feel: **Uneasy** about safety and young workers while current income remains secure.
S1.quote: A computer's green mark cannot hold a temporary stair rail under a worker's hand.
fieldNote: He keeps **never-using-AI** consistent and presses for a physical sign-off rule through an actual union safety meeting.
The change threatens **young workers' shifts** and handover safety; he does not predict his own immediate wage loss.

steps.text: Record rail faults and paid fixing time on two civic-site floors
Ask union safety meeting for named worker stair sign-off

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI by 2028 could draw the temporary stairs, then capable robots around 2031 might build them. The contractor should publish paid crew numbers and fund safe training before cutting people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about 63 when robots can do the hands-on work, four years before I hope to leave regular sites if retirement income allows. If my own carpentry shifts shrink, four months saved and some local builders would not cover a long wait for wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll take the crew's concern to our union branch and ask for written staffing, a safe robot trial and advance notice. If my paid shifts are cut, I'll apply only to posted local carpentry roles with safe work, regular hours and pay that covers our bills; my partner and I will check our retirement statements first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible wage gap at 63, with enough savings to search but not to stop working. I won't call a retirement enquiry an exit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grown children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our grown children we are checking the numbers before asking them for anything. They should be free to manage their own households.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What safety checks would a robot stair trial need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot stair trial needs a grounded test flight, a clear area and a worker with a stop switch. A load test must come before another trade climbs it.

say: **2028 thinking AI** draws stairs before robots build them around 2031.
Builders owe workers **paid crew figures** and safe training terms.
think: At about **63**, robot stair work could shrink my paid shifts.
Four months of **savings** and some nearby builders cannot fund years without wages.
do: **Ask** union branch for written staffing, safe trial and advance notice.
**Review** retirement statements against bills with partner.
**Apply** after cuts to posted local carpentry job with safe regular bill-covering pay.
feel: **Anxious** about a realistic wage gap before affordable retirement.
S2.quote: If my own carpentry shifts shrink, four months saved and some local builders would not cover a long wait for wages.
fieldNote: His own **paid hours** could shrink at about 63, so the mood rises to anxious despite a four-month reserve.
The fallback application requires **actual cuts** and posted local carpentry work with safe duties, regular hours and bill-covering pay.

steps.text: Ask union branch for written staffing, safe trial and advance notice
Review retirement statements against household bills with partner
Apply after cuts to posted local carpentry job with safe regular bill-covering pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2031 could draw the stairs and robots around 2034 could assemble them. Five years is enough for a proper rail test and a funded path into site inspection for people whose shifts change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about 66 when robots do the physical work, around a year before I hope to leave if our income covers the bills. If retirement figures fall short, I may still need a full carpenter wage and cannot take unpaid course days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the union training group to press for a recognised stair-safety inspection course with funded fees, a real place and full pay during class. If the builder signs those terms, I'll enrol next intake; after qualifying, if my hours are cut and retirement income is short, I'll apply only to posted local inspection jobs with safe duties, regular hours and bill-covering wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible last-year wage cut, though five years lets us bargain. I would learn inspection work on paid time, but I will not start using AI simply because a robot arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would an inspection course assess?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The course should test a real temporary stair, including handrail load and a safe stop before other trades use it. A classroom talk alone will not qualify me to sign a site handover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What terms would let you take it and later change jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wage must stay at its normal level through class days, with the assessment fee paid too. A posted local inspection job must show the hours and enough pay for our bills before I leave this crew.

say: **2031 thinking AI** changes plans before robots build stairs around 2034.
A **funded inspection course** and real rail tests need written terms.
think: At about **66**, retirement may work if income covers our bills.
If figures fall short, I still need **paid site work** without unpaid study days.
do: **Ask** union training group for funded stair-inspection course and full class pay.
**Enrol** if recognised course has signed fees, real place and full class wages.
**Apply** after qualification and cuts if income short to posted local inspection job with safe bill-covering hours.
feel: **Anxious** about a possible wage gap, with paid-training time to prepare.
S3.quote: A classroom talk alone will not qualify me to sign a site handover.
fieldNote: He considers **actual conditional enrolment** in traditional site inspection, without claiming to learn or use AI.
Course and applications retain **funded fees** and full pay; later applications need qualification, cuts and posted local safe bill-covering work.

steps.text: Ask union training group for funded stair-inspection course and full class pay
Enrol if recognised course has signed fees, real place and full class wages
Apply after qualification, cuts and income shortfall to posted local safe inspection job with bill-covering pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2036 may draw stair plans and robots around 2039 may build them. A decade gives the trade time to pay apprentices to learn rail checks from a real carpenter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about 71 when robots do the physical stair work, beyond my hoped-for exit around 67. Our four-month reserve does not guarantee retirement, so my partner and I will check income figures each year instead of announcing a date today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep leading the present stair crew and checking rails while I am employed. At the union apprenticeship committee I'll propose paid practice on a grounded stair; if our income allows leaving around 67, I'll hand the rail-fault log to a younger fitter before the last shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about whether retirement income will be enough, although robots at 71 would likely come after my work. I can leave a safety habit without pretending I will still be on site in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show an apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the apprentice how to pull the rail and watch the anchor move, then write the result beside the stair number. A robot's tidy checklist cannot feel a loose handrail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the committee make practice paid and safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The committee request will specify paid apprentice hours, a supervised ground-level stair and a fitter signing each test. I'd bring our current log so the builder sees the actual faults.

say: **2036 thinking AI** draws plans before robots build stairs around 2039.
**Paid apprenticeships** should preserve real rail-load testing.
think: At about **71**, robots may arrive after my hoped-for exit at 67.
The **four-month reserve** still leaves retirement affordability to actual statements.
do: **Keep** leading current stair crew and checking handrails.
**Propose** paid supervised rail practice at union apprenticeship committee.
**Hand** rail-fault log to younger fitter before exit if income permits.
feel: **Uneasy** about retirement affordability, with time for a safe handover.
S4.quote: A robot's tidy checklist cannot feel a loose handrail.
fieldNote: His **present site work** and pre-exit handover remain separate from the robot date at about 71.
The **union apprenticeship plan** names paid hours, a supervised ground-level stair and a fitter's sign-off.

steps.text: Keep leading current stair crew and checking handrails
Propose paid supervised rail practice at union apprenticeship committee
Hand rail-fault log to younger fitter before exit if income permits

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because stair robots around 2031 could cut paid hours when I would be about 63, years before an affordable exit. A written crew plan, paid safety training and actual posted local work with adequate wages would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who signs for the temporary stairs after a machine builds them. A handrail can be neat in a drawing and still move when a worker grabs it. The last test belongs to someone on site.

headlineQuote: A handrail can be neat in a drawing and still move when a worker grabs it.
portrait: **Ben**, 58, leads temporary-stair carpentry with a vocational certificate and strong practical skill at ordinary trade pay.
He and his postal-office partner have a **four-month reserve**; their children are grown and some local building alternatives exist.
He has **never used AI**, prefers direct rail checks and asks a union committee for paid safety practice.
Fast robots make him **anxious** about wages before a conditional exit around 67; later change allows a supervised handover.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring stair robots around 2031 while he would be about 63 and still need wages.
whatWouldHelp: A **written crew plan**, paid safety training and posted local roles with adequate wages would help bridge any shortfall.
